name: The Wait-Time Verifier
oneLiner: Measures the assistant's real answer latency and checks it against the 'estimated wait' range the app displays.
lead: While the assistant is thinking, the app shows a range like 'Wait time: about 5 to 10 seconds.' This agent verifies that promise: it fires questions across a size spectrum, scrapes the displayed range, times the actual latency to a tenth of a second via Playwright, and flags any estimate the real wait blew past.
chore: The manual version: sit with a stopwatch, type a question, read the estimate, start timing on Enter, stop when the answer appears. Repeating that across short questions, long essay prompts, and everything between is tedious and imprecise — human timing is off by seconds, and nobody wants to babysit fifty prompts by hand.
instead: The agent fires a whole library of differently-sized questions, scrapes the on-screen estimate for each, times the real wait to the tenth of a second, and marks whether the actual latency fell inside the promised range. It also captures screenshots throughout, as evidence of what the screen showed at each moment.
whyItMatters: If the app keeps promising '5 seconds' but takes 40, users lose patience and trust; catching that gap early keeps the estimate believable.

howItWorks.step: Loads the built-in library of short, medium, long, and very-long questions (or a custom pipe-separated list from the CLI), tagged by category.
howItWorks.explain: A hand-rolled arg loop, and the two defaults are deliberate: `env` defaults to `'dev'` (the safe target) and `headless` defaults to `false` so the **first run is visible** — you need to watch it to sign in. The value flags use `args[++i]` to consume the *next* token as their argument, advancing the loop index in place. `--prompts` splits on `|` because spaces can't delimit prompts that themselves contain spaces — a pipe is a safe separator for free-text questions. The whole question set is a **fallback**: `ALL_PROMPTS` (the built-in short→very-long library) is used unless the user supplied custom prompts, and each custom prompt is `.trim()`-ed and tagged `'Custom'` so it still flows through the same category-grouped reporting as the built-ins.

howItWorks.step: Launches Playwright Chromium and navigates to the app, reusing a cached storage-state so most runs skip sign-in.
howItWorks.explain: The environment maps through `ENV_URLS[env]` so `--env` picks the target with no hard-coded address in the flow. Auth is **conditionally injected** via the spread `...(hasAuth ? { storageState: authFile } : {})` — an idiom that adds the `storageState` key only when the saved session file exists, giving a clean context on the very first run and a silent-login context thereafter. The **fixed 1920×1080 viewport** matters for this agent specifically: the 'Wait time' note and the processing indicators must be reliably on-screen to scrape, and a stable large viewport keeps their layout consistent across runs so a timing screenshot is comparable. The `goto` waits only for `domcontentloaded` (not `networkidle`) because this app streams and background-polls — `networkidle` may never fire — and sign-in is handled downstream **only** if the navigation actually lands on a login page.

howItWorks.step: Types the question, presses Enter, starts a `Date.now()` timer, and scrapes the on-screen 'Wait time: about X to Y seconds' range.
howItWorks.explain: Measurement accuracy hinges on **where the clock starts**: `startMs = Date.now()` is captured *between* `fill` and `press('Enter')`, so the fill time (which isn't part of the app's latency) is excluded and timing begins at the exact instant the user's action commits. The wait-time note is scraped with a **case-insensitive text locator** (`text=/Wait time/i`) rather than a brittle CSS path, and a 15s `waitFor` allows for the note appearing slightly after submit. The range regex `(\d+)\s*[-–]\s*(\d+)` matches **both** an ASCII hyphen and a Unicode en-dash (`–`) because UIs often render ranges with the typographic dash — missing that would drop every estimate. Critically it's guarded by `if (match)`: when no range is found `displayedWaitRange` stays unset, which is what lets a later step report 'no estimate shown' instead of comparing against a bogus range.

howItWorks.step: Polls until the thinking/analyzing/wait indicators all disappear to mark the real wait, then keeps polling until the answer text length holds steady to mark total time.
howItWorks.explain: This deliberately measures **two different things**. The first loop defines the *wait* — the moment the app stops promising and starts answering — as the point where **all three** processing signals (thinking, analyzing, and the 'Wait time' note itself) are simultaneously gone; requiring all three prevents calling it early when one indicator lingers. `actualWaitSec` is stamped there, which is the number compared against the promised range. The second loop then measures *total render time* by a **stability heuristic**: the answer's text length must hold identical for **3 consecutive 1s reads**, and any growth resets `stableCount` to 0, so a mid-stream pause can't be mistaken for completion. Each visibility read is `.catch(() => false)` so a transient locator error reads as 'indicator gone' rather than throwing. The verdict is a plain inclusive-bounds check (`>= lo && <= hi`) against the scraped range — deterministic, so the same latency always grades the same way.

howItWorks.step: Checkpoints the JSON after every question, then builds a color-coded Excel report grouped by category with a per-category pass rate.
howItWorks.explain: The JSON is **rewritten after every single prompt**, not once at the end — this is a checkpoint, so a crash or a hang on prompt 40 of 50 still leaves the first 39 results on disk (the run is long and includes deliberately slow very-long questions, so losing it all would be costly). Each write includes a `completed` count so a partial file is self-describing. The per-category summary tests `withinRange === true` with a **strict equality** rather than a truthy check, which is intentional: a prompt with *no* estimate shown has `withinRange` unset/`undefined`, and this excludes it from the in-range tally instead of miscounting it as a pass — the pass rate reflects only prompts that actually had a promise to keep. `categoryOrder` fixes the row order so short→very-long reads intuitively in the workbook.

examples.caption: A quick factual question
examples.input: 'What's the capital of France?' — the app shows 'Wait time: about 2 to 6 seconds.'
examples.output: The real answer starts in 3.4s. Marked INSIDE range, green, with a screenshot of the estimate.

examples.caption: A long report-writing request
examples.input: A prompt for a 2000-word status report — the app shows 'Wait time: about 20 to 40 seconds.'
examples.output: The real wait is 71s. Marked OUTSIDE range, red — so the tester can flag the estimate as too optimistic for long tasks.

examples.caption: An answer with no displayed estimate
examples.input: A medium question where the app never renders a 'Wait time' note.
examples.output: The agent still times the real latency but records status 'no estimate shown', so a missing promise is visible rather than silently ignored.

underHood.heading: Loads the question library
underHood.input: A built-in set of short/medium/long/very-long questions — or a custom pipe-separated CLI list.
underHood.output: An ordered, category-tagged list of questions ready for timing.

underHood.heading: Opens the app — no token needed
underHood.input: A cached storage-state file, if a previous run left one.
underHood.output: A ready-to-chat Chromium page — falling back to interactive sign-in only on an actual redirect to a login screen.

underHood.heading: Times each answer twice
underHood.whenRuns: Once per question, right after Enter.
underHood.input: The moment the question is submitted.
underHood.output: Two readings: time to the first sign of a real answer, and time until the answer stops growing.

underHood.heading: Checks the promise against reality
underHood.whenRuns: Right after each answer finishes rendering.
underHood.input: The scraped 'Wait time: X to Y seconds' range and the two measured times.
underHood.output: An inside/outside verdict for that question, plus a screenshot trail taken every few seconds while it waited.

underHood.heading: Builds the report
underHood.whenRuns: After every question in the library has run.
underHood.input: Every timing result, grouped by category.
underHood.output: A color-coded Excel workbook (green = inside range, red = outside, yellow = no estimate shown) plus a JSON backup and per-category accuracy.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
An app login — the agent navigates straight to the app and only stops for sign-in on an actual redirect to a login page.
No content prep: a built-in library of sample questions ships with the agent, short to very-long, so it runs out of the box.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime the agent runs on.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program; Node executes it. One-time setup per machine.
steps.firstRun: Only needed on a fresh machine.

steps.label: Install the agent's dependencies, then Playwright in its sibling folder.
steps.cmd:
cd path/to/the-agents
npm install

# the browser-clicking library lives in its own sibling folder:
cd Playwright
npm install
steps.why: The root install pulls the ExcelJS writer and the `tsx` runner. The second pulls in Playwright — which opens the app, types the question, and watches the screen.
steps.firstRun: Downloads everything (a minute or two, longer the first time Playwright fetches its Chromium binary).

steps.label: (Optional) set an SSO password if your login uses one.
steps.why: The agent goes straight to the app; on a redirect to a company SSO page it tries this password automatically. Leave it unset and sign in by hand the first time — either way the storage-state gets saved for next time.

steps.label: Run against the target environment.
steps.why: The actual run. A visible Chromium window opens, asks each library question in turn, scrapes the on-screen estimate, times the real latency to a tenth of a second, and screenshots throughout.
steps.firstRun: A browser opens; sign in when prompted (or it uses the password above). A full run can take a while — the library includes deliberately slow, very-long-response questions.
steps.rerun: Add `--headless` once signed in, so it runs invisibly: `npx tsx agents/time-range-verification-agent.ts --env dev --headless`.

steps.label: Open the report.
steps.why: A color-coded workbook — green for latencies inside the promised range, red for outside — grouped by category, plus a screenshots tab and a full screenshot folder.

inputs.name: --headless
inputs.desc: Run invisibly in the background instead of showing the browser window.

inputs.name: --prompts "A|B|C"
inputs.desc: Run your own pipe-separated question list instead of the built-in library.

inputs.name: --offset / --limit / --worker-id
inputs.desc: Shard the library across parallel runs — useful for a big batch.

inputs.name: environment variables
inputs.desc: An optional SSO password, only if your login has one.

outputs.name: WaitTime_<env>_<timestamp>.json
outputs.desc: Every question's displayed wait-time range, the two measured times, and the inside/outside verdict.

outputs.name: WaitTime_<env>_<timestamp>.xlsx
outputs.desc: A color-coded, category-grouped report with a per-category accuracy percentage and a screenshots tab.

outputs.name: screenshots_<env>_<timestamp>/
outputs.desc: A full folder of screenshots — the prompt, the wait-time note, the processing state every few seconds, and the finished answer.

runbook.rerun: Every run times every question fresh — nothing is cached but the login session. It's built to shard: run four workers in parallel, each with a different `--offset`/`--limit`/`--worker-id`, and merge the reports after.
runbook.integrate: Run it nightly (or post-deploy) against QA and watch the per-category accuracy over time. An estimate that used to hold and now doesn't is exactly the quiet regression this catches before users notice.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: watch the agent ask a question, read the app's wait-time promise, and time the real answer against it.
script: Open a terminal beside the app so viewers see the browser the agent controls.
Say: 'This agent checks whether the assistant's own wait-time estimate is honest. Watch.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Show the two `npm install` runs — the agent's own libraries, then the browser-automation library in its sibling folder.
Mention the optional sign-in password variable, then say most people just log in by hand the first time.
Run the command for one environment; narrate the browser opening and signing in.
Point at the 'Wait time: about X to Y seconds' note the moment it appears on screen.
Let one short question and one very-long question run; narrate the stopwatch and the screenshots being taken every few seconds.
Open the finished spreadsheet; point at a green (inside range) row and a red (outside range) row.
Close: 'Every promise the app makes about how long it'll take, checked against the clock — automatically.'
